“April 7. I woke early and finally saw, to my great joy, what must have been the North Pole. There was no doubt about it: the Pole lay directly beneath me. Sadly, I was now so far above it that I could not see anything in clear detail. I considered the rising figures for my altitude recorded between six in the morning on April 2 and eight forty that same morning, when the barometer stopped registering. From those figures, I could reasonably estimate that by four this morning, April 7, the balloon stood at least 7,254 miles above sea level. This height may seem immense, but the calculation probably placed me far lower than I actually was. Whatever my exact height, I could certainly see the earth’s entire widest diameter. The whole northern hemisphere lay below like a map drawn from a view straight overhead, and the circle of the equator formed the boundary of my horizon. Your Excellencies will understand that the small unexplored regions inside the Arctic Circle were still too small and too distant for me to study them closely. They lay right beneath me, so their shapes were not shortened by viewing them at an angle, but that did not overcome the distance. Even so, what I could see was unusual and exciting. Beyond the enormous rim I mentioned earlier—which, with slight exceptions, marked how far human exploration had reached in this area—a nearly unbroken sheet of ice extended northward. Over its first few degrees, the surface grew noticeably flatter. Farther north it sank into a level plain, then curved inward quite deeply. At the Pole itself it ended in a clearly outlined circular center. From the balloon, this circle’s width appeared to cover about sixty-five seconds of arc. Its shade changed, but it was always darker than any other part of the hemisphere I could see. Sometimes it turned entirely black, so dark that nothing could be made out within it. I could learn little beyond this. By noon the circle’s outline had become much smaller, and by seven in the evening I could no longer see it. The balloon had passed over the western edge of the ice and was floating quickly toward the equator.

“April 8. The earth’s apparent width was noticeably smaller today. Its overall color and appearance had also changed considerably.

When Mr. Hiram B. Otis, the American Minister, bought Canterville Chase, everyone said he was making a foolish mistake. The house was unquestionably haunted. Even Lord Canterville, a man who took honesty extremely seriously, felt obliged to tell Mr. Otis when they discussed the sale.

“We have not wanted to live there ourselves,” Lord Canterville said, “since my great-aunt, the Dowager Duchess of Bolton, had such a fright that she suffered a fit and never fully recovered. Two skeletal hands were placed on her shoulders while she was dressing for dinner. I must tell you, Mr. Otis, that several living members of my family have seen the ghost. So has our parish rector, the Reverend Augustus Dampier, a Fellow of King’s College, Cambridge. After the Duchess’s unfortunate experience, none of the younger servants would remain. Lady Canterville often slept very little because of the mysterious noises from the corridor and library.”

“My lord,” the Minister replied, “I will buy the ghost along with the furniture at whatever they are worth. I come from a modern country where we have everything money can buy. Our energetic young men are out enjoying themselves all over Europe and carrying off your finest actresses and leading singers. I reckon that if Europe had a ghost, we would soon have it back home, either in a public museum or traveling around as an exhibition.”

“I’m afraid the ghost does exist,” Lord Canterville said with a smile, “even if it has resisted your enterprising showmen’s offers. It has been well known for three centuries—since 1584, in fact—and always appears before anyone in our family dies.”

“Well, so does the family doctor, Lord Canterville. But ghosts do not exist, sir, and I doubt the laws of nature will make an exception for the British aristocracy.”

“You Americans are certainly very natural,” replied Lord Canterville, who had not quite understood the last remark. “If you do not mind having a ghost in the house, all is well. Just remember that I warned you.”

The purchase was completed a few weeks later. At the end of the social season, the Minister and his family moved to Canterville Chase. Mrs. Otis, formerly Miss Lucretia R. Tappan of West 53rd Street, had once been a celebrated beauty in New York society. Now middle-aged, she was still a very handsome woman, with beautiful eyes and a superb profile.

“In fact, I haven’t mentioned the most important one.”

“What is it, Harry?” the young man asked wearily.

“The obvious consolation: taking another woman’s admirer after losing your own. In fashionable society, that always clears a woman’s reputation. But really, Dorian, Sibyl Vane must have been unlike any of the women we meet. I find something quite beautiful in her death. I’m glad to live in an age when such extraordinary things happen. They make one believe that the things we all play at—romance, passion, love—can actually be real.”

“I was terribly cruel to her. You’re forgetting that.”

“I’m afraid women appreciate cruelty, outright cruelty, more than anything. Their instincts are wonderfully primitive. We have liberated them, but they remain slaves searching for masters. They love being controlled. I’m sure you were magnificent. I’ve never seen you completely furious, but I can imagine how beautiful you looked. Besides, something you told me the day before yesterday seemed fanciful then, but now I realize it was absolutely true. It explains everything.”

“What did I say, Harry?”

“You told me Sibyl Vane embodied every romantic heroine for you: Desdemona one evening, Ophelia the next. If she died as Juliet, she returned to life as Imogen.”

“She’ll never return to life now,” the young man muttered, hiding his face in his hands.

“No, she won’t. She has played her final role. But think of that lonely death in the shabby dressing room simply as a strange, lurid episode in a Jacobean tragedy, a magnificent scene by Webster, Ford, or Cyril Tourneur. The girl never truly lived, so she has never truly died. To you, at least, she was always a dream, a ghost drifting through Shakespeare’s plays and making them more beautiful by being there, a reed through which his music sounded richer and more joyful. The instant she encountered real life, she spoiled it, and it spoiled her, and so she disappeared. Mourn Ophelia if you wish. Cover your head with ashes because Cordelia was strangled. Protest to heaven because Brabantio’s daughter died. But don’t spend your tears on Sibyl Vane. She was less real than any of them.”

Silence followed. Evening deepened in the room. Shadows stole in from the garden without a sound, on silver feet. The colors of objects faded away, as though exhausted.

After a while, Dorian Gray raised his head.
